To show the inner order of the process that leads to this coincidence—to show the necessity of this final coincidence between the standpoint being studied and the standpoint of the one studying it—is to justify the latter standpoint. It is to prove its truth, and therefore the truth of the content that depends on it.
But that content is not only the systematic Philosophy that must be written from this standpoint. It is also Phenomenology itself, taken as a whole.

From Phenomenology’s own point of view, its standpoint remains unchanged from beginning to end. What changes are only the false standpoints that it studies, not the true standpoint from which it studies them.
At the beginning of Phenomenology, these standpoints are very far apart. As the work progresses, they gradually converge, until at the end they coincide.
Yet the standpoint reached at the end of Phenomenology is the same standpoint from which Phenomenology began.

It therefore seems as though Phenomenology presupposes and anticipates its own conclusion from the very start—even though, from its own point of view, that conclusion can be reached only by passing through everything that lies between beginning and end.

In other words, the phenomenologist becomes a philosopher only after he has written—or thought through—Phenomenology from beginning to end. But at the same time, unless he is already a philosopher, unless he already knows what philosophy is and what its task consists in, he cannot write or think a Phenomenology in the first place. He cannot even begin one—that is, undertake the task and conceive its “project.”

The very purpose Phenomenology sets itself therefore leads necessarily to what logic calls a “vicious circle” (vitiosus circulus). It presupposes from the outset what it hopes to prove at the end, and it can prove it only because it has already presupposed it.

There is no doubt that this “circle” exists. And we can state explicitly that it is absolutely unavoidable in philosophy, so long as philosophy seeks to be genuinely philosophical knowledge: knowledge that is absolutely true, fully concrete, and therefore complete.
Every other field of knowledge either deals with abstractions or is not concerned with truth.

Pure mathematics, for example, is concerned only with what makes deductions from wholly arbitrary premises—its “axioms” or “postulates”—logically valid. These premises are not in themselves true or false. All they need to be is “consistent,” meaning free of internal contradiction.

The so-called “real” sciences, such as physics and biology, deal only with a part of concrete reality, or with one partial aspect of it. They must therefore always begin with certain propositions that they simply accept “on faith” and never prove, because those propositions lie beyond the part or aspect of reality that the science itself studies.

All the real sciences, for example, accept “without proof” that a reality exists independently of our consciousness and that this reality can “reveal itself” through our discourse, provided that discourse obeys certain logical laws.
For philosophy, by contrast, reality, consciousness, discourse, the laws governing discourse, and so on are not simply “facts” or “axioms.” They are questions whose answers must themselves be proved.

But in attempting to prove these things, the philosopher necessarily has to use at least discourse itself and its logical laws. So when he tries to prove their truth, he necessarily falls into a “vicious circle.”

Because philosophy seeks concrete knowledge, it seeks omniscience: knowledge of everything that can in any way be known. And because it seeks knowledge, it accepts nothing merely “on faith.” It tries to “show” or “prove” the truth of everything it claims.
It therefore seeks rigorous proof of everything.
Yet whenever it offers a proof, it is clear that it must already presuppose some part of what it is trying to prove.
With Hegel, philosophy became fully aware of the necessity of this logical circle.
But instead of treating the circle as “vicious,” Hegelian philosophy sees its “circularity” as the distinctive sign of perfect knowledge—of its completeness or wholeness.

By returning, at the end of its regular internal or dialectical development, to its own beginning, philosophy shows that it has exhausted all of its possibilities. It can therefore neither be expanded nor altered.
And this means that it is absolutely and definitively true: complete or perfect as knowledge.

From the standpoint of “formal logic”—that is, of the laws governing discourse—the circularity of philosophy means only that it is not its isolated propositions that are individually “true” or “proved.” What is true is philosophy as a whole, philosophy in its entirety.
Only the truth of the whole guarantees or “proves” the truth of its parts, even though the whole obviously could not exist without those parts.

Each individual element of the philosophical system may not be convincing by itself. But if the system as a whole is convincing, and if that system can stand only through the elements that actually make it up, then those elements ultimately prove convincing as well—precisely because the system presupposes them from the beginning.

That this philosophical “circularity” is perfectly compatible with truth becomes clear once we notice that the same kind of “circularity” exists in reality itself—and can therefore also exist in the way reality is “revealed” through discourse, which is to say, in truth.
Philosophy presupposes what it proves in the same sense that any whole presupposes its parts, while those parts in turn presuppose the whole.

Obviously, an ellipse presupposes its parts—its segments—because without them it could not exist. But those parts, insofar as they are parts of an ellipse, also presuppose the ellipse itself. Without the ellipse, they could not exist as what they are.
We might suppose that the ellipse is made up of geometrical points that “exist” independently of it. But this is not really so.

At every point on an ellipse, we can draw a tangent—that is, a straight line. The point in question therefore belongs at once to a point, a straight line, and an ellipse. At each of its points, then, the ellipse can coincide with a straight line.
So where is the ellipse actually elliptical—that is, curved?

Clearly, the components or elements of an ellipse, as an ellipse, are not points but segments, however tiny those segments may be—“differentials.” And these segments cannot exist as segments of the ellipse without the ellipse itself.
A dog is obviously made up of parts—a head, legs, a tail, and so on—and could not exist without them. In that sense, the dog’s existence “presupposes” its parts.
But equally, the dog is not made up of a head, legs, and a tail “in general.” It is made up of a dog’s head, a dog’s legs, and so on.

The parts of a dog therefore presuppose, so to speak, the dog itself. They cannot exist without it or apart from it. Or take the classic problem of the chicken and the egg. The chicken presupposes the chicken egg from which it hatched, while the egg in turn presupposes the chicken that laid it.

Of course, we usually bring up this problem precisely to show that we do not really understand where the chicken ultimately came from. So one might raise the same objection against circular philosophy. Even if such a philosophy is possible—that is, even if it contains no contradiction—its origin still seems impossible to understand. We might grant that, in a system that had somehow “fallen from the sky,” the whole could prove the truth of the parts that make it up. But we would still have no idea how that whole could ever have been constructed in the first place. How, in other words, can someone who reaches the philosophical point of view only at the end of Phenomenology write the Phenomenology at all, when he apparently has to possess that point of view from the very beginning?

In reality, there is nothing incredible or impossible about this. The same thing happens whenever we arrive at genuine knowledge: there is a kind of circular dependence between a “hypothesis” and the technical or revolutionary test that verifies it.

Take an example we have already used: the invention of the first airplane. The airplane could fly only if the design was correct. But the design became demonstrably correct only when the airplane actually flew.

Exactly the same applies to the philosopher. He constructs his systematic Philosophy on the basis of a project that he assumes to be true. He then establishes or “proves” its truth through the “success” of the completed system. In this sense, the philosopher’s “work”—the actual completion of the philosophical system—is itself, so to speak, an experimental or technical test of the system’s truth, and therefore of the truth of the elements it initially had to presuppose. To this technical test through work is then added a “revolutionary” test: the public recognition that the philosopher’s system receives.
What is true of the system as a whole is also true of its parts, and especially of Phenomenology.

Until the phenomenologist has finished his work, he cannot be certain that his starting point was correct or that the conclusions he reached along the way were true. Only the completed work, by displaying the convincing force of the whole, can finally convince him that he began in the right place and never strayed from the right path.

If we like, we can say that when the phenomenologist—and the philosopher—begins his work, he takes a “risk,” and that his success is therefore “contingent.” But this risk is smaller, say, than the one taken by the engineer who built the first airplane, and his success is correspondingly less contingent.

We can call this unavoidable element of “contingency” ability, talent, or even genius, depending on the scale of the risk involved—that is, on the possibility of failure. But even where the risk is enormous, success is neither incredible nor miraculous.

It would be miraculous only if the phenomenologist genuinely began “from the beginning,” with no help from the work of his predecessors. It would have been miraculous, for example, if Hegel’s Phenomenology had appeared in the Athens of Pericles or in the hut of an Australian “Aborigine.” It would have been equally miraculous for a workable design for an airplane to have appeared there.

But we do not have to travel the whole road again every time. We need only travel a small new section of it—indeed, a very small section in comparison with the whole—which extends a path that others have already cleared.

Of course, while travelling this new but short stretch of road, one may discover that from the point now reached it would be better to take a different route. In other words, someone who reaches that point may open up a new and very long path. Yet even then, he can do so only because the road leading to that point had already been cleared.

We must not forget that every phenomenon that “breaks with the series” still presupposes the series from which it breaks away. The scale of the “risk” Hegel took may justify calling the “contingency” that enabled him to write his Phenomenology an act of genius. But we should remember that he owed no less to his philosophical predecessors than, say, the Wright brothers owed to theirs in pure and applied mechanics.
In any case, the “circularity” remains. If we like, we can call it a kind of “circular guarantee” within Phenomenology.

For its author, this has a practical meaning: he could not write it correctly “in one go.” He had to write it, so to speak, circularly. Having reached the end, he had to go back and correct the beginning. Starting again from that corrected beginning, he then had to revise the end and the path leading to it, and so on, until the work formed a whole that was genuinely convincing.

For the reader, the same circularity means that Phenomenology can be fully understood in all its parts only after it has been read in its entirety. Yet the whole obviously cannot be understood unless its parts have been understood. Reading it must therefore also be “circular.” Strictly speaking, only a second reading can be fully convincing.
And this means that Phenomenology can properly be criticized only as a whole, not by tearing isolated passages out of it.
2. The theme and object of a Phenomenology
Having established the aim—or aims—of a Phenomenology, we must now determine its theme. That means identifying its object: what it studies, and what kind of true knowledge it claims to provide.

But we must not make it seem as though the phenomenologist simply chooses his subject at random. We need to show that the introductory first part of the philosophical system could not have any object other than the one chosen by Hegel’s Phenomenology—and by mine.

So we must connect the theme of Phenomenology with its purpose. In defining its object, we have to show that once Phenomenology sets itself the goals described above, it is necessarily led to this particular object and no other.
We should not forget, however, that only Phenomenology itself can ultimately justify the phenomenologist’s choice of these goals.
As we have seen, the purpose of Phenomenology is to prepare us for philosophical knowledge: true knowledge of concrete reality.
Strictly speaking, philosophical knowledge is philosophical precisely because it is concrete, unlike “scientific” knowledge in the narrower sense, which deals with abstractions.

But if we use the word science more broadly and contrast scientific knowledge—as convincing and secure, that is, necessary and universal—with the contingent information possessed by ordinary people, then philosophical knowledge must first of all also be scientific knowledge.
It is scientific precisely because it is knowledge (epistēmē) rather than opinion (doxa).
And what distinguishes knowledge from opinion is the presence of self-consciousness, or conscious awareness of what one knows.
A person who merely holds an opinion cannot, on the basis of that opinion itself, know that it is only an opinion. For no clear reason, he may simply take it to be genuine knowledge.
Knowledge is different. Genuine knowledge itself shows the person who possesses it that he possesses knowledge—and why what he possesses really is knowledge.

That is to say, it shows itself to be true knowledge: knowledge of truth, or of reality itself as reality reveals its own essence to human beings through the meaningful content of coherent, intelligible human speech.
Someone who possesses knowledge knows that he possesses it. Conversely, only someone who knows that what he possesses really is knowledge can truly be said to possess knowledge.
But we can know that we possess knowledge only if we know what knowledge is.
Knowledge of what knowledge is therefore a necessary condition for possessing knowledge at all—and, as we will see, it is also a sufficient condition.

Now, the aim of Phenomenology is to make philosophical knowledge possible, and Phenomenology itself claims to be a necessary preliminary condition for possessing that knowledge. We must therefore say that Phenomenology is nothing other than knowledge of what knowledge is.
In other words, if its aim is to create the real possibility of actually possessing knowledge, then knowledge itself must necessarily become the theme of its investigation.
The object of Phenomenology is therefore knowledge as such.
It studies knowledge in order to acquire knowledge of knowledge as knowledge. In this sense, it is a “discourse on knowledge”—an epistemo-logy: a science of knowledge, or a theory of knowledge.

And since the possession of knowledge, together with the process by which it is acquired, is called cognition (gnōsis), Phenomenology can also be defined as a “discourse on cognition”—a gnoseo-logy: a science or theory of cognition.

The theme of Phenomenology therefore coincides with the theme of Kant’s three famous Critiques. Their object—both Kant’s Critiques and Phenomenology—is human knowledge and the process of cognition that makes this knowledge possible. They make cognition their theme because their goal is to prepare the way for philosophical knowledge.
Kant was the first to formulate clearly the principle that philosophical knowledge is impossible without some prior knowledge of what knowledge is and of the process of cognition that leads to it.
Kant’s reasoning was roughly this. In order to possess a truth—that is, a true content of knowledge—we must first understand the form taken by that content: knowledge and cognition as such.

Or, to put it another way, cognition is the instrument by which we reach truth, which is the content of knowledge. So we can hope to reach truth only if we first turn our attention to this instrument and study it.

On the one hand, once the Critiques have taught us what cognition is, we can determine the limits of cognition and therefore establish what can and cannot become the content of true knowledge—that is, what can count as truth.

On the other hand, once we understand the instrument itself, we can take account of the changes or distortions caused by its use. We will then stop attributing to the objective content of knowledge—that is, to truth—features that in fact belong only to its subjective form: to human knowledge and the process of human cognition.
This formulation of the theme of a “theory of cognition” appears explicitly for the first time in Kant.
But the idea that knowledge of human knowing must in some sense come before the content of philosophical knowledge is as old as philosophy itself.

In one sense, the distinction between knowledge and opinion was already the theme of all Plato’s Dialogues. The works attributed to Aristotle and collected under the title Organon—works that served throughout the Middle Ages as an “introduction to philosophy”—are devoted to the study of knowledge and cognition as a means of reaching truth.

Likewise, at the beginning of modern philosophy, Descartes devoted two of his earliest philosophical works to the study of knowledge and cognition: the Discourse on Method and the Meditations on First Philosophy.
More generally, one can find “gnoseological” investigations in every major philosopher. In that sense, the theme of Phenomenology is a traditional philosophical theme.

Still, we must emphasize again that Kant was the first to understand clearly the full significance and fundamental necessity of this preliminary investigation into cognition. He showed not merely that such an investigation conditions the possibility of philosophical knowledge, but that it in some sense determines the whole character of that knowledge.
In this respect, the true “father” of Phenomenology is Kant.
Yet although the themes of Phenomenology—whether Hegel’s or mine—and of Kant’s Critiques are identical, we must not overlook a fundamental difference between them.
They study the same object—human knowledge and cognition—but they differ radically in how they define, understand, and interpret that object.
Hegel accused Kant of having an “idealist” understanding of cognition and knowledge.

Kant himself objected to being counted among the “idealists.” And it is true that he never went so far as idealism in the strict sense: the absurd claim that only consciousness and the processes occurring within it exist, while outside consciousness and independently of it there is no reality at all.

Still, Hegel was right in the sense that Kant’s thought undeniably contains idealist tendencies and distortions. It is certainly no accident that the neo-Kantians who were so widespread at the end of the nineteenth century and the beginning of the twentieth were hardened “idealists.”

For the purposes of his investigation, Kant was entirely right to distinguish between the form and content of truth—that is, between knowledge and cognition on the one hand and the reality they express on the other.
But he seems to have forgotten that, in actual fact, the two are inseparable, and that when we study them separately we are dealing only with abstractions.

Kant nowhere says that subjective knowledge can exist independently of objective reality or outside it. Yet in his account the subject who knows begins to resemble a kind of “consciousness in general,” composed of intuition, understanding, and reason, whose relation to reality remains obscure.

This consciousness starts to look suspiciously like the “mind,” “soul,” or “world-reason” of the rationalist philosophers: something that derives the whole content of its consciousness from itself, a priori, rather than from the reality that exists outside it.
In any case, Kant treats it as possible to study consciousness, knowledge, and cognition as such, independently of the reality revealed in and through them.
So although he allows part of the content of knowledge to come somehow from reality, he still locates another part—the a priori or “immanent” content—within consciousness independently of reality.

Conversely, while Kant rightly maintains that reality exists independently of consciousness and cognition, he forgets that the reality we are actually talking about includes, as a matter of fact, our consciousness and cognition of that reality.
